name: L-Carnitine

lead: L-carnitine is a compound synthesised in the liver and kidneys from lysine and methionine and obtained from foods such as red meat. It is sold as a supplement, often in the forms L-carnitine tartrate or acetyl-L-carnitine, for fat loss, exercise recovery and energy.
Its physiological role is well established, but supplementation in people who are not deficient has produced modest and inconsistent effects on weight and body composition across meta-analyses.

paras: Carnitine carries long-chain fatty acids across the inner mitochondrial membrane so they can be oxidised for energy, and it buffers excess acetyl groups. Oral supplementation raises plasma levels but does not reliably raise muscle carnitine in healthy people without additional measures, which may explain the weak results.

Intakes of about 2 to 3 g daily are generally tolerated, with nausea, diarrhoea and a fishy body odour at higher intakes. Gut bacteria convert carnitine to trimethylamine, which the liver turns into TMAO, a compound associated with cardiovascular risk in observational studies, though causality is unresolved. It is sold as a supplement and is unscheduled in most places.
